Question: If human eyes in perfect condition are cameras, how much megapixels would it have? Would it have noise? Would it be considered the best camera known for mankind? Would it work best for low light conditions?
Answer: Human eyes are, in fact, biological cameras. They can see at about 324 megapixels, or about 170 DPI at a distance of 20″. Yes, it has noise. You can notice it better when trying to see things at very dark places. There is technology available to build electronic cameras with higher resolution, zoom, night vision, and other features that the human eye lacks. However, the greatest feature we have is image processing. What your mind sees is not simply what your eyes are capturing. The brain collects parallax information to build a 3D model of the scene in front of you. The eyes are constantly moving and scanning, to form a perception with a much higher resolution and detail than the eye would capture if it were a still camera. It corrects color, increases dynamic range (difference between the darkest and brightest places you can perceive at the same time), and so on. That is why there is no commercial available camera that comes anywhere near to what we can see with our naked eyes.

Question: What is a "flat spin" in aviation?
Answer: First, try to visualize a regular spin. It usually happens when one wing stalls while the other is still generating enough lift. This results in a dive where the plane is rotating around its longitudinal axis. Now, let’s say the tail of this plane is heavier than is should be (due to bad weight distribution or other factor). If it is heavy enough, it may end up being pulled down, causing the plane to be leveled with the horizon, but still falling vertically (while rotating like a boomerang). If checked carefully, you can notice that all control surfaces (ailerons and stabilizers) will be ineffective, as the air flows perpendicular to them (90 degrees angle of attack). There is also the Inverted Flat Spin, which is even more dangerous: For most airplanes out there, a flat spin is an impossible to recover situation, because all pilot inputs will be of no effect. There are heroic tales about pilots from World War I that had to unstrap themselves in mid-flight and jump from the back to the front seat in order to shift the center of gravity forwards, and therefore recover from a flat spin (I don’t have any reliable sources on this). Some acrobatic planes can recover from flat spins by using excessive thrust, torque or any other means available. Even in those cases it is still considered a very dangerous maneuver.

Question: If all GPS fails, how would a pilot flying over the Pacific or Atlantic (or even over land) find an airport to land his plane safely?
Answer: Without GPS, you could get around by using radio direction finding. There are lots of these spread around the continents: This is a VOR antenna. It emits a signal that enables the receiver to calculate which direction the radio waves are coming from (among other things). There are other types of antennas and signals used. There are thousands of those around the world. They are usually near airports, and there are navigation charts indicating their positions and frequencies. In some cases, even commercial radio broadcasters (the same ones you would listen to on your car) could be used to track position. But if that fails, you could use an Inertial Reference System. That one above is from a ballistic missile, but modern airliners all have similar systems. It’s like sitting on a wheelchair blindfolded while someone moves you around, and then trying to guess your position. I know you will quickly lose track, but that’s because our inner ear isn’t that much good. A high precision gyroscope with a few accelerometers (way better than those on your smartphone) can keep precision within a few meters even after several hours of flight. The best part of that system is that it is fully autonomous, not depending on anything outside the aircraft to work (except during calibration, usually done before the flight). If all that fails, you can still use dead reckoning (calculating position based on direction, speed and time). And, if the sky is clear, there is also celestial navigation, although most countries do not teach that in flight schools anymore.

Question: Will commercial space travel one day be as cheap as like taking airplane today?
Answer: The honest answer is that no one really knows. People love to say things like “120 years ago we didn’t have airplanes, now we went to the moon”, and that leads to a wrong conclusion that we will keep evolving that fast and in another hundred years a trip to mars will be like a trip to Pittsburgh. The missing piece here is that technological evolution often comes in leaps. Once man discovered fire, it didn’t take many decades until they found so many uses to it, and then they spent the next thousand years without learning anything new. The same applies to the Industrial Revolution, Information Revolution, and so on. Ten years ago you would buy a new computer and 6 months later it would be completely obsolete and useless compared to what was hitting the market then. It is not true anymore. This means in a thousand years, we will probably not have flying cars, teleportation, no final cure for cancer, and no hover boards. Am I sure of all this? Absolutely not. There’s always the chance someone will invent/discover something no one ever thought of, and it will trigger another revolution. There is no guarantee it will happen within a thousand years though, or even a million, or ever happen at all. We can dream, but space is really, really big.

Question: If Earth were truly a globe, would airline pilots constantly have to adjust their controls so as not to fly off into space?
Answer: First, the Earth is a globe. Second, yes, it requires constant adjustments. For every 60 nautical miles the airplane flies in a straight line, it has to pitch down 1 degree. But since pilots have to make constant adjustments to keep the plane leveled and maintain altitude, and since 1 small degree over 60 miles is impossible for a human being to notice, those adjustments come out as noise. Some advanced autopilot equipment can detect that change, and they are calibrated to take that into consideration. Imagine you are driving your car, and there is a 1 degree left turn ahead. I bet most people wouldn’t even notice it. Now, spread that turn over a distance of 60 miles. You can use instruments to detect that the turn actually exists, but there’s this friend who insists the road is straight because he cannot see a sharp turn there… Lastly, if no adjustments were made, it would not fly into space. Every plane has an altitude ceiling, and from there it would no longer be able to climb. Edit: As was pointed out in the comments, airplanes have longitudinal static stability, which means the 1 degree correction over 60 miles will happen without pilot input.

Question: Would it be possible for an almost perfectly made paper plane to fly around the world if it had the ideal environmental conditions?
Answer: Paper planes are gliders (Glider (aircraft)). They don't have thrust, meaning they rely on air currents to maintain altitude (while maintaining airspeed), or else aerodynamic drag will eventually cause them to hit the ground. They also don't have maneuverability, which makes it even harder because asymmetrical currents will cause it to roll uncontrolled. You could design it to stabilize itself, but it would only work until a certain limit. Throwing a paper plane to a transcontinental flight would not only require a perfect design, but also perfect winds, which I would guess would be one chance in a billion.

Question: Is the way Denzel Washington’s character in Flight (2012) saves the plane, crew, and its passengers really possible in a real world scenario?
Answer: No. These are the problems I could pick up in the dive and crash scene: - On several occasions you see the yoke going fully to the front. That would cause a dive much more intense than shown in the movie, and a negative G that would violently throw every object to the ceiling (including people without seat belts). - You see the captain on the yoke telling the first officer to control the thrust. On a real operation one of them would be controlling both yoke and thrust, and the other would be trying to identify the problem and fixing or circumventing it by performing emergency checklists. - The first officer says "I have no control on my side". Most airplanes have both sides mechanically connected, which means moving one yoke would cause the other to move together. There would be no sense in one side having control and the other not having. The exception would be a Fly-by-wire system, but I can't tell you if it's the case because the airplane model in the movie is fictional (looks like an MD-80, but it's different in many ways). - That "revert to manual control" switch to pull and rotate, I've never seen a plane with that. But again, it's a fictional plane. - The inverted part... Airliners are very heavy. They have wings designed to generate lots of positive lift. To fly upside down, acrobatic planes are designed so they can generate enough negative lift. With that much weight and enormous wings generating positive lift, going inverted would cause them to actually sink a lot faster. There's a point he says "we are leveled, we can maintain altitude like this". That would not happen. Also, structural forces caused by the maneuver could rip the plane apart, tearing control surfaces and even wings. - Fire on the left engine... He puts it out. That procedure on a real plane would shut the engine down immediately. Then, fire in the right engine, same thing. Yet, right after that, he asks Margaret for full power. And when the camera zooms on the ECAM (which monitors the engines), you can see both EGTs going up to the limits, and N1 levels are also very high, meaning both engines would be working. Later both N1 indicators go down together, as if both engines failed at the same time. - Then he is gliding. Is the elevator working normally now? - Airplanes are designed to be as light as possible. This means they have fragile structures. They can withstand strong aerodynamic forces, but a wing tip versus a church tower, at gliding speed, guess which one will break. - He doesn't flare for the landing. The camera shows him pulling the yoke when it's actually too late.

Question: If you could only view 2 faces of the Rubik's cube is it possible to determine the colors of the remaining 4 faces?
Answer: Did you mean a scrambled cube? No, it is not possible to determine the colors without seeing them. The hidden faces could hold an absurd number of combinations. But if you mean a solved cube, then it depends. Are you familiar with that specific cube? Most cubes have no pink face. But nothing is stopping someone from making one with all the colors they like. That way, you have no way to tell if the bottom face is purple, gray or antique fuchsia. But if it's a familiar and solved cube, then it is totally possible. The center pieces of a Rubik Cube cannot change position. This means if the cube you are holding now has the center white piece opposite to the center yellow piece, you can arrange it in any way you want, and these pieces will still be in opposite places. Most "default" cubes today are like: Top: Yellow Bottom: White Front: Blue Back: Green Right: Red Left: Orange So if you are seeing top and front faces (yellow and blue), you already know the positions of all other colors. If you see a left red and a front yellow, then the color at the right is orange. And so on.

Question: Theoretically, if you had a hole through the center of the earth would it be more effective to launch rockets into space by first dropping them through the other side?
Answer: No. First, if you reach 25,020 mph while inside the atmosphere, you will face enormous air drag. It would make you decelerate VERY quickly, and most likely destroy your rocket in the process (the escape velocity formula only works in a vacuum). Now let's say Earth has no atmosphere. The escape velocity is calculated from the surface. If you reach 25,020 mph while inside that planet hole, you would not escape Earth. Without thrust you would reach the other side with zero speed. This means your momentum cannot be conserved, except by burning the same amount of fuel you would by launching stationary from the ground.

Question: How can I prevent bots from filling my form? I have a website and bots are always sending ads through my site to my email.
Answer: You can use captchas or other similar solutions. However, if your site is small (a personal blog for example), you can solve it in a simple way. Add a hidden empty field to your form, and use javascript to fill it with a keyword of your choice when the page loads. Now, when you receive data from that form, check for that keyword. If it's not there, it was probably a bot (because they don't process javascript), and you should ignore all his inputs. Of course that solution will not work on a large scale site because people would simply reprogram their bots to target your site specifically.
